title: Traditional IP Network Address Translator (Traditional NAT)
subtitle: How a whole private network shares one public IP address, one port at a time.
summary: Traditional NAT lets hosts that use private IP addresses reach the outside Internet through a border router that rewrites their packets. Basic NAT swaps one IP address for another, while NAPT also rewrites TCP/UDP ports (or ICMP query IDs) so many hosts can share a single public address. The RFC obsoletes RFC 1631, fixes its checksum algorithm and spells out the limits of the approach.

plainLanguage.summary: Traditional NAT lets hosts with private IP addresses reach the Internet through a border router that rewrites their packets. Basic NAT swaps one IP address for another. NAPT also rewrites TCP or UDP ports, so many hosts can share one public address. The RFC obsoletes RFC 1631, corrects its checksum algorithm and states the limits of the approach.

questions: what is the difference between basic nat and napt
how does napt share one ip address
how is the checksum updated when nat changes an address
what are private ip address ranges

tldr.problem: A network's internal addresses often cannot be used outside it, and changing providers or backbones would mean renumbering every host, yet many hosts only need to start sessions to the outside.
tldr.mechanism: A border router rewrites addresses (Basic NAT) or address plus TCP/UDP port or ICMP query ID (NAPT) on every packet, keeps a binding table for each session, and patches the IP, TCP, UDP and ICMP checksums.
tldr.outcome: Private networks can reach the Internet through one or a few public addresses with no changes to hosts, at the cost of end-to-end addressing, inbound connections and some protocols.

sections.title: Introduction and Motivation
sections.content:
The RFC starts from a simple observation: sometimes a network's internal addresses cannot be used outside it, either for privacy or because they are not valid there. External topology also changes. Customers switch providers, backbones are reorganized, and every time that happens the addresses inside the local domain would have to change too. A single address translation router can hide those changes from the inside.

Small Office, Home Office (SOHO) users are the other driver. They often have several machines running TCP/UDP applications but only one address from their provider, assigned to the remote access router. NAPT lets all of those machines use that one address at the same time.

The RFC is upfront about the price. The solution takes away the end-to-end significance of an IP address and makes up for it with increased state in the network. As a result, end-to-end IP-level security such as IPsec cannot be assumed between end hosts when a NAT device sits on the path. The advantage is that it can be installed without changes to hosts or routers.

Address translation is application independent, but it is often accompanied by application level gateways (ALGs) that inspect and alter payloads. FTP is the most popular ALG on NAT devices. Terms such as address realm and ALG are defined in RFC 2663, which this document leans on throughout. It extends the idea first introduced in RFC 1631.
sections.plainLanguage: NAT is useful when a network's internal addresses cannot be used outside it, or when changing providers would force every internal address to change. Small offices often have several machines but only one provider address, and NAPT lets them all share it. The cost is that an IP address no longer identifies one host end to end, so end-to-end security such as IPsec cannot be assumed. Hosts and routers need no changes.

sections.title: Traditional NAT: the big picture
sections.content:
"Traditional NAT" is the name this RFC gives to two variations: Basic NAT and NAPT. In both, sessions are unidirectional, outbound from the private network. Sessions in the opposite direction are allowed only on an exceptional basis, using static address maps for pre-selected hosts.

Only the stub border router, the router that sits between the stub domain's LAN and the WAN link to the regional or provider router, may be configured to perform translation (the RFC's Figure 1).

Basic NAT
Translation is limited to IP addresses. A pool of globally valid addresses is dynamically mapped to private ones, and individual private hosts can be given static mappings.
NAPT
Translation covers the IP address and the transport identifier: a TCP/UDP port or an ICMP query ID. Many private addresses can share one public address.

Because the stub router is the only place translation happens, it is mandatory that every request and response for a session pass through the same NAT router. With more than one exit point, the routers must share the same translation table, which the RFC notes means exchanging state information if flows are to survive a failover.
sections.plainLanguage: Traditional NAT has two forms, Basic NAT and NAPT. In both, sessions start from the private network and go outward. Inbound sessions are allowed only through static address mappings for chosen hosts. Only the border router of the private network translates, so all packets of a session must pass through that one NAT router.

sections.title: Basic NAT
sections.content:
In Basic NAT, a stub domain with private addresses talks to the outside by dynamically mapping its private addresses onto a set of globally valid ones. If there are at least as many global addresses as local nodes, every node is guaranteed a mapping. Otherwise, the number of nodes that can reach the outside at once is limited by the size of the global set. Individual private addresses can instead be mapped statically to a specific global address, either to guarantee access to the outside or to let the outside reach a local host at a fixed public address. Multiple simultaneous sessions from one local node reuse the same mapping.

The RFC's Figure 2 shows two stubs that both use the private block 10.0.0.0/8. Stub A's NAT owns the class C block 198.76.29.0/24 and stub B's owns 198.76.28.0/24. Host 10.33.96.5 in stub A sends to 198.76.28.4, the globally unique address for stub B's host 10.81.13.22. Stub A's NAT rewrites the source to 198.76.29.7 on the way out, and stub B's NAT rewrites the destination to 10.81.13.22 on arrival. Return packets go through the reverse translations.

Addresses inside a stub are local to it, so the same private block can be reused by any number of stub domains. The global addresses given to each NAT, though, must be unique.

Notice that neither the hosts nor the ordinary routers need any change. As far as the stub A host is concerned, 198.76.28.4 simply is the address of the host in stub B.
sections.plainLanguage: Basic NAT maps private addresses onto a pool of globally valid addresses. If the pool is smaller than the number of hosts, only that many hosts can reach the outside at once. A private address can also be mapped statically to one fixed global address. Several private networks can reuse the same private block, but the global addresses each NAT owns must be unique.

sections.title: NAPT: many hosts, one address
sections.content:
NAPT maps tuples of (local IP address, local TU port) to tuples of (registered IP address, assigned TU port). "TU port" means a TCP or UDP port. This fits SOHO sites that have just one provider-assigned address, and the registered address can be the same as the router's own WAN interface address.

In the RFC's Figure 3, the stub router's WAN interface has address 138.76.28.4. Host 10.0.0.10 opens a telnet session to 138.76.29.7 from TCP port 3017. The router rewrites the source to 138.76.28.4 and a uniquely assigned port, say 1024, before forwarding. The reply arrives addressed to 138.76.28.4 port 1024 and is rewritten to 10.0.0.10 port 3017.

ICMP query packets are handled the same way. The identifier field is set by the query sender and returned unchanged in the response, so the (local IP address, local query ID) tuple is mapped to a (registered address, assigned query ID) tuple. ICMP error messages need extra work, covered below.

Only TCP, UDP and ICMP query sessions are allowed from local nodes. Other session types are simply not permitted through a NAPT router. Inbound sessions are assumed to be for the NAT router itself unless the target service port is statically mapped to a local node, which is how a well-known service such as DNS can be exposed.
sections.plainLanguage: NAPT maps a private address and port to a public address and an assigned port. The router rewrites the source address and port on outgoing packets and reverses this on replies, so many hosts can share one public address. ICMP queries are handled the same way using the query ID. Only TCP, UDP and ICMP query sessions are allowed from local hosts.

sections.title: Bindings and the life of a session
sections.content:
The translation phases are the ones described in RFC 2663. This RFC adds what is specific to traditional NAT.

Address binding. In Basic NAT, a private address is bound to an external address when the first outgoing session starts from that host. Every later outgoing session from the same private address reuses the binding. In NAPT the binding is from (private address, private TU port) to (assigned address, assigned TU port), again created by the first outgoing session. An application might open several simultaneous sessions from the same private tuple; one binding can then serve all of them.

Lookup and translation. Once a binding exists, soft state may be kept for each connection using it, and each packet is looked up against its session for translation.

Unbinding. When the last session using a binding ends, the binding itself may be terminated.

Because the binding is created by an outbound packet, an unsolicited inbound packet has nothing to match. That is the source of the privacy property in section 6.1 of the RFC and also the reason that inbound access needs static maps.
sections.plainLanguage: The first outgoing session from a private address creates a binding that links it to an external address. In NAPT the binding also covers the port. Later sessions from the same address or port reuse it, and it can end when the last session using it ends. An unsolicited inbound packet matches no binding, so inbound access requires static mappings.

sections.title: What gets rewritten in each packet
sections.content:
In Basic NAT, every packet's IP header is modified: the source address on outbound packets, the destination address on inbound ones, and the IP header checksum. TCP and UDP checksums must also be updated because they cover a pseudo header that contains the IP addresses. As an exception, a UDP header with a zero checksum should not be modified. ICMP query checksums do not cover IP addresses, so no ICMP change is needed in Basic NAT.

NAPT does the same, plus it translates the TCP/UDP port (source on outbound, destination on inbound). For ICMP queries it replaces the query ID and fixes the ICMP checksum.

ICMP errors are more involved because they carry part of the original packet. The outer IP header, the ICMP checksum, the embedded IP header's address and checksum all change, and under NAPT so does the TU port or query ID in the embedded header.

FTP needs an ALG that watches the control session for PORT commands and PASV responses, since they carry addresses (and under NAPT, ports) as ASCII octets. Rewriting changes their length, so the ALG keeps a table of TCP sequence and acknowledgement deltas: sequence numbers are incremented outbound and acknowledgement numbers decremented inbound.

DNS may need no ALG if internal servers hold internal names and external servers hold only external ones. IP options such as Record Route and source routes may be left unsupported or untranslated, which exposes private addresses but should not break the path.
sections.plainLanguage: In Basic NAT, the router changes the IP addresses in each packet and updates the IP, TCP and UDP checksums. NAPT also changes port numbers or ICMP query IDs. ICMP errors need extra work because they contain part of the original packet. FTP needs an application level gateway (ALG) that rewrites addresses written in its control messages.

sections.title: Checksum adjustment
sections.content:
Translation happens on every packet, so it must be cheap. Rewriting an address would seem to force a full checksum recomputation, but IP, TCP, UDP and ICMP all use a one's complement sum. It is therefore enough to compute the arithmetic difference between the old and new values and add that to the existing checksum.

The RFC gives sample C code, checksumadjust, which takes a pointer to the checksum, the old data and its length, and the new data and its length. It subtracts the old 16-bit words from the (complemented) checksum, adds the new ones, folds carries, and complements the result again.

The algorithm applies only to even offsets and even lengths: the pointer to the old data must sit at an even offset from the start of the header, and both lengths must be even.

Correcting this algorithm is one of the stated reasons RFC 3022 exists. The Preface says it corrects the checksum adjustment algorithm published in RFC 1631. The routine is reproduced below exactly as printed in the RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: NAT changes every packet, so checksum updates must be cheap. Because the checksums use a one's complement sum, the router only needs to add the difference between the old and new values, not recompute the whole checksum. The RFC includes sample C code for this. Correcting the algorithm published in RFC 1631 is one reason this RFC exists.

sections.title: Limitations and security
sections.content:
The general limits of NAT are in RFC 2663. This RFC lists the ones specific to traditional NAT.

Privacy and debugging. Sessions are unidirectional from private hosts, and external hosts never see the real addresses, so NAT can be viewed as a privacy mechanism. The same property makes problems harder to trace. If an inside host sends spam or attacks a machine, the address visible outside is the NAT router's.

ARP on the LAN side. If the WAN link is replaced by a LAN and the NAT address pool lies in that LAN's subnet, the router must answer ARP requests for the mapped global addresses with its own MAC address under Basic NAT, since no other node owns them. The authors suggest vendors may optionally support proxy ARP.

Fragments under NAPT. Outbound fragmented TCP/UDP packets are "doomed to fail". Only the first fragment carries the port numbers, and two private hosts might use the same fragment ID toward the same destination, corrupting both sessions.

Other issues. Private and global address spaces must not overlap. The NAT must not advertise private networks to the backbone. When a Basic NAT pool is used up, it may optionally switch the last global address to NAPT, though applications that worked before may then break. Traffic that is encrypted defeats ALGs. The Security Considerations section simply defers to RFC 2663 and says its considerations apply to traditional NAT.
sections.plainLanguage: Because outside hosts never see the real addresses, NAT works as a privacy mechanism, but it also makes problems harder to trace. Fragmented TCP or UDP packets under NAPT are "doomed to fail", since only the first fragment carries the port numbers. Private and global address spaces must not overlap. Encrypted traffic defeats ALGs. The security section defers to RFC 2663.

items.title: Hidden sources
items.text: Real addresses are not visible outside, which helps privacy but makes tracing abuse harder.

items.title: Fragments
items.text: Outbound TCP/UDP fragments under NAPT fail because only the first has port numbers.

items.title: ARP duty
items.text: A Basic NAT router on a shared LAN must answer ARP for the mapped global addresses.

items.title: End-to-end broken
items.text: Per-session state in the router; IPsec end to end cannot be assumed; encrypted payloads defeat ALGs.

today: NAPT is what almost every home and small-office router does: all devices on the LAN share one public IPv4 address from the provider. Operators also run large-scale NAT in their own networks as IPv4 addresses ran short (see RFC 6888). Later RFCs refined the behaviour this document describes, notably RFC 4787 for UDP and RFC 5382 for TCP. The private blocks it cites come from RFC 1918.
